name: Microsoft SharePoint
toolCategory: General-purpose document management and intranet platform

verdict.line: Not a vendor bake-off — SharePoint is where the buyer's policies already sit, so this is a displacement conversation about content and attestation evidence, never a feature shootout against Microsoft.
verdict.doInstead: Do not attack SharePoint. Let the buyer keep it for files. Ask who writes and updates the policy text today, and who can produce a timestamped acknowledgment record per employee per version at audit — that is the wedge, not document storage.

size.value: Not published for the SharePoint product specifically

pricing.value: Bundled in most Microsoft 365 business and enterprise plans; standalone SharePoint plans are published by Microsoft. The buyer almost always already pays for it, so incremental cost is effectively zero in their mind.

positioning.value: Microsoft positions SharePoint as "The knowledge platform for Copilot and agents" — content management, AI-powered search, secure sharing and branded intranet hubs.

strengths.text: Already paid for and already deployed at most multifamily operators as part of Microsoft 365 — no new vendor, no new procurement, no new login.

Genuine full-content search: SharePoint indexes the text inside documents, not just titles and metadata, and Microsoft markets AI-powered search that "understands intent and surfaces relevant files and answers."
Mature document versioning, content approval and check-out controls are documented native capabilities.
Unlimited flexibility — permissions, retention, audit policies and Power Automate workflows can be shaped to almost any process.

gaps.text: Microsoft's own document management overview covers versioning, content approval, check-out, retention and audit policies, and does not describe a built-in policy attestation or acknowledgment-tracking feature.

Microsoft's SharePoint product page markets content management, search, sharing and intranet capabilities; it does not offer prewritten policy content of any kind, let alone multifamily policy text — the buyer supplies every word.

Third-party assessment of plain SharePoint for policy management states it "cannot natively ask employees to read and acknowledge a policy, track who has and has not done so, or produce an audit log of attestations," and that there is "no native alert system that tells you a policy is about to expire and needs review" — both require Power Automate configuration or custom development.

whyWeWin: Grace Hill ships the policies. SharePoint ships an empty library. Our Policies library is over a thousand customizable policies, forms and job descriptions written by multifamily experts across 18+ manuals — the buyer starts from written content, not a blank Word document.

Grace Hill maintains regulatory currency as part of the subscription. With SharePoint, somebody on the buyer's payroll owns rewriting the fair housing, leasing and tax-credit language every time a rule changes — and that person usually does not exist.

Attestation evidence is the product, not a workflow the buyer has to build. Grace Hill captures secure electronic acknowledgments tied to a policy version and a person, and assigns automatically by location, position, group or employee.
Policy-to-training linkage lives in PerformanceHQ: the policy the employee acknowledged and the course that teaches it are in the same system, reportable together.
The real cost of SharePoint is not the license. It is the internal author, the Power Automate build, and the person who has to reconstruct an acknowledgment trail from email when a claim lands.
askThis: Who on your team actually writes the policy language today, and when was the emergency-procedures or fair-housing section last rewritten?
If a fair housing complaint came in tomorrow, how long would it take you to produce proof that this specific employee acknowledged this specific version of that policy on a specific date?
When a state rule changes, who finds out, and who edits the document? What is the lag between the rule changing and your manual changing?
Your SharePoint search finds the document. Can it tell a leasing agent the answer to a question at 4pm on a Friday, or does it hand them a 60-page PDF?
How many of your properties are working from a copy of the manual that is no longer the current version?
Did somebody build the acknowledgment workflow in Power Automate? Who maintains it when they leave?

objections.objection: We already have SharePoint and it's free.
objections.response: Agreed — keep it. SharePoint is a good place to store files. What it does not give you is the words. You are still paying somebody to write and re-write every policy, and to rebuild the acknowledgment trail by hand. We ship over a thousand multifamily policies already written and keep them current. Compare our fee to the cost of the person doing that job now.

objections.objection: Our IT team can build acknowledgment tracking in Power Automate.
objections.response: They probably can. The question is whether they should own it for the next five years, and whether the flow they build will hold up as evidence — version-locked, per-person, timestamped — when your counsel asks for it. That is a maintenance liability you would be taking on to avoid a subscription.

objections.objection: SharePoint search already finds anything.
objections.response: It does — SharePoint content search is genuinely strong, and we're not going to claim otherwise. But search only works on what's written. If the policy text in there is three years old and does not reflect current fair housing guidance, great search just finds the wrong answer faster.

doNotSay: Do not say SharePoint has no search or bad search — it indexes document content and is one of the strongest search engines in this whole comparison set. Claiming otherwise destroys credibility with any IT stakeholder in the room.
Do not say SharePoint 'can't' do attestation. It cannot do it natively, but it can be built. Say 'not native — somebody has to build and maintain it.'
Do not position this as Grace Hill vs. Microsoft. The buyer keeps SharePoint. We are replacing the empty policy folder inside it.
Never disparage the customer's IT team or their existing build.

po-regulatory-updates.note: Microsoft supplies software, not policy text. Any regulatory currency is the customer's own work.

po-jurisdiction-variants.note: No policy content is supplied, so no jurisdiction variants exist to supply.

po-attestation.note: Not described as a native feature in Microsoft's document management overview; commonly built with Power Automate, custom lists or a third-party app.

po-esignature.note: Microsoft's document management overview does not describe policy e-signature; organizations typically integrate a third-party e-signature service.

po-overdue-reporting.note: Third-party assessment reports no native policy-expiry alerting; review reminders and overdue escalation require Power Automate configuration.

po-position-assignment.note: Granular permissions and audience targeting by Entra ID group; not policy-assignment-by-position out of the box.

po-training-linkage.note: Policy-to-course linkage is not part of SharePoint; Microsoft offers Viva Learning as a separate product.

founded.value: Not published on the vendor site

ownership.value: Owned by NEOGOV. Warburg Pincus and Carlyle announced an agreement to sell NEOGOV to EQT X and CPP Investments on July 28, 2025; deal value not disclosed in the announcement.

size.value: NEOGOV states it serves nearly 10,000 public sector organizations; employee count not disclosed in the announcement.

positioning.value: "A complete public safety management system, built with AI for public safety to bring critical workflows into one platform, helping agencies operate more efficiently and make better decisions."

strengths.text: Deep, purpose-built policy mechanics: version control with archived prior versions, side-by-side change comparison with color-coded highlights, e-signature and acknowledgment tracking, and audit trails.
Full-text keyword search across the policy library, plus a mobile app for staff who are not at desks.
Training assignment linked to policies and job roles, so acknowledgment and instruction connect in one system.
Partner content ecosystem for its own market — accreditation standards manuals and a Lexipol integration for prewritten public safety policy content.
Backed by NEOGOV, which serves nearly 10,000 public sector organizations — real scale and institutional durability behind the product.

gaps.text: PowerDMS markets itself to public safety (law enforcement, 9-1-1, fire, EMS, corrections), healthcare accreditation, government and corporate. Multifamily housing is not among the named markets on its site.

The prewritten policy content available through PowerDMS is public-safety oriented — accreditation standards manuals and a Lexipol integration. No multifamily policy content library is described in its product materials.
Pricing is not published; buyers must request a quote.

whyWeWin: PowerDMS is an excellent system waiting to be filled. Grace Hill arrives with over a thousand multifamily policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals already written by multifamily experts — the buyer is live on day one, not after a six-month internal writing project.

Our content is maintained for multifamily regulatory change — fair housing, leasing, tax credit compliance, emergency procedures. A public-safety content ecosystem does not cover a single one of those.
Policies and training sit in the same PerformanceHQ platform with the same reporting, and both are multifamily-specific — the policy and the course that teaches it were written by the same people.
Assignment by location, position, group or employee maps to how a multifamily portfolio is actually organized: properties, regions, roles.
askThis: Their policy content partners write for police departments and hospitals. Who would write your fair housing, leasing and tax-credit language?
If you buy PowerDMS, what is your plan for the first 90 days — do you have manuals ready to load, or would somebody be writing them from scratch?
When HUD guidance or a state landlord-tenant rule changes, does PowerDMS notify you and update the text, or does that land on your compliance team?
How many multifamily operators are on their reference list, and can you speak to one?
What does implementation include — do they migrate and structure your existing manuals, or is loading content on you?

objections.objection: PowerDMS has better policy workflow features than you do.
objections.response: They have a mature policy engine and we don't dispute that. But every feature they have operates on text somebody still has to write. We give you the text — over a thousand multifamily policies already written and kept current — plus the acknowledgment, version and assignment machinery. Ask yourself which half is harder to build in-house.

objections.objection: They already work with big organizations, so they can handle multifamily.
objections.response: They can technically. The question is content. Their prewritten library and partner ecosystem are built for accreditation and public safety standards. Nothing in it speaks to fair housing, tax credit compliance or unit turns. You would be buying a very good empty container.

doNotSay: Do not claim PowerDMS lacks policy management features — it has version control, redlining, e-signature, acknowledgment tracking and full-text search, all documented publicly.

Do not say PowerDMS has no prewritten content — it does, through accreditation standards manuals and a Lexipol integration. The accurate claim is that the content is public-safety oriented, not multifamily.
Do not state PowerDMS pricing or claim it is more or less expensive than Grace Hill — pricing is not published.

strengths.text: Runs as an app on Microsoft 365 SharePoint Online with integration into Word Online, Outlook, Teams and Active Directory — no new platform for IT to adopt and no new place for staff to log in.
Full policy lifecycle: version history and audit trails, approval workflows, a dedicated acknowledgment module, e-signature integration and quiz-on-content capability.

Now backed by Ideagen, an established compliance software group, which adds institutional depth behind the product.

Pricing is not published; buyers must request a demo or quote.

whyWeWin: ConvergePoint upgrades the container. Grace Hill fills it. We ship over a thousand multifamily policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals written by multifamily experts — a buyer choosing ConvergePoint still has to write every word of every policy.

Grace Hill maintains regulatory currency for multifamily as part of the subscription. A horizontal SharePoint compliance app has no view into HUD guidance, fair housing enforcement trends or state landlord-tenant change.
Policy and training live in one multifamily platform in PerformanceHQ, written by the same subject matter experts, reportable together.

name: The Status Quo — shared drive, binder, and email acknowledgments
aka: The binder in the leasing office
Word docs on the S: drive
toolCategory: No system — shared drive, printed binder, and email or paper sign-off

verdict.line: The most common competitor and the hardest to beat — it costs nothing, works well enough on a normal Tuesday, and fails only on the day it matters most.

pricing.value: No subscription cost. The real cost is staff time to write and maintain policies, plus unquantified risk exposure — neither of which appears on any budget line.

positioning.value: "We already have policies. They're on the shared drive."

strengths.text: Zero subscription cost. There is no line item, no renewal, no procurement cycle, and no budget conversation to lose. For an operator watching every dollar, this is a genuinely rational default.
Simple and universally understood. Everyone knows how to open a Word document, print a page, and reply 'received' to an email. There is no adoption curve and no change management project.
No training required. Nobody has to learn a new system, remember a new login, or sit through an onboarding webinar. Onsite teams already have enough software to log into.
Total control and total flexibility. The policies say exactly what leadership wants them to say, in the company's own voice, and can be changed in thirty seconds by anyone with edit access.
It has worked so far. Most operators running this way have never had an incident where it failed, which makes the risk feel theoretical and the spend feel unnecessary.

gaps.text: Nobody owns regulatory currency. Policies are updated when someone remembers or when something goes wrong, so the manual drifts further from current fair housing and housing compliance guidance every year it sits untouched.

No single current version. Copies proliferate across property folders, laptops, printed binders and email attachments, and there is no way to know which properties are working from an outdated manual.

Acknowledgment evidence is not defensible. An email reply saying 'got it' does not establish which version of which policy the employee received, and reconstructing that trail after a complaint means searching mailboxes of people who may no longer work there.
No overdue visibility. There is no way to answer 'which employees at which properties have not acknowledged the current policy' without someone building a spreadsheet by hand.
New hires and transfers fall through. Onboarding acknowledgment depends on an individual manager remembering to send the file, which fails silently and is invisible until an audit.
Policy and training are disconnected. There is no way to show that the person who acknowledged the fair housing policy also completed the fair housing course.
The hidden labor cost is real but invisible. Someone on staff writes and rewrites this content, and that cost never shows up next to the zero on the subscription line.

whyWeWin: The buyer's real problem is not storage — it is authorship. Grace Hill ships over a thousand customizable multifamily policies, forms and job descriptions across 18+ manuals, written by multifamily experts, covering emergency procedures, leasing, tax credit compliance, maintenance and operations. The status quo supplies a folder; we supply the content.

Grace Hill owns keeping the content current as multifamily regulation changes. In the status quo, that job belongs to a person who already has a full-time job, which is why the manual is three years old.

Secure electronic acknowledgments create a digital paper trail tying a named employee to a specific policy version on a specific date — the artifact counsel asks for, produced in seconds instead of reconstructed from email.
Automatic assignment by location, position, group or employee means new hires and transfers get the right policies without a manager remembering to send anything.
Policies and training live together in PerformanceHQ, so the acknowledgment and the course that teaches the behavior report as one story.
askThis: When was your policy manual last updated, and who did it?
If a fair housing complaint landed tomorrow, how long would it take you to prove this employee acknowledged this version of that policy on a specific date — and where would you look?
How many of your properties are working from a copy that is no longer current? How would you find out?
Who acknowledged the last policy update, and who didn't? Can you pull that in the next five minutes?
When you hired someone last month, what guaranteed they received and acknowledged the current policies?
How many hours a year does your compliance or ops person spend rewriting policy language — and what would they do with that time instead?
When a leasing consultant has a policy question at 4pm on a Friday, what do they actually do?

objections.objection: We already have policies. They're on the shared drive.
objections.response: I believe you — almost everyone does. Two questions though. When were they last updated for current fair housing guidance, and if a complaint came in tomorrow, could you produce proof that a specific employee acknowledged a specific version on a specific date? Those are the two moments the shared drive can't cover.

objections.objection: This has worked fine for us for years.
objections.response: That's usually true right up until it isn't. The shared drive works every day except the one day you need evidence. We're not selling you insurance against a hypothetical — we're selling you back the hours your team spends writing policy language, plus a record you can actually produce.

objections.objection: We can't justify the cost when what we have is free.
objections.response: It isn't free — it's unbilled. Somebody on your payroll writes and rewrites those manuals, and that time is real money that just never gets counted. Add up those hours, then compare. And that's before you price a single hour of counsel's time reconstructing an acknowledgment trail from email.

objections.objection: Our attorney reviewed our handbook last year.
objections.response: That's more than most operators do. Was it your operations manuals too — fair housing procedures, leasing, tax credit files, emergency response? And what is the plan for keeping them current between reviews? A one-time review is a snapshot; regulation keeps moving.

doNotSay: Do not tell a prospect their current approach is negligent, reckless, or that they are exposed to lawsuits. It insults the person you are selling to, and it is a legal characterization we are not qualified to make.

Do not invent or cite a statistic about fair housing settlement amounts, litigation frequency, or the cost of non-compliance. If we do not have an approved sourced figure, use the customer's own numbers instead.
Do not claim Grace Hill Policies eliminates legal risk or guarantees compliance. We supply content and evidence; we do not provide legal advice.
Do not mock the binder. Many buyers built it themselves and are proud of it. Respect the effort, then show what it cannot do.
